{{Short description|Theorem in complex analysis}}
{{Complex analysis sidebar}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Borel–Carathéodory theorem''' in [[complex analysis]] shows that an [[analytic function]] may be [[Bounded function|bounded]] by its [[real part]]. It is an application of the [[maximum modulus principle]]. It is named for [[Émile Borel]] and [[Constantin Carathéodory]].

== Statement of the theorem ==

Let a function <math>f</math> be analytic on a [[closed disc]] of [[radius]] ''R'' centered at the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]]. Suppose that ''r'' < ''R''. Then, we have the following inequality:

:<math> \|f\|_r \le \frac{2r}{R-r} \sup_{|z| \le R} \operatorname{Re} f(z) + \frac{R+r}{R-r} |f(0)|. </math>

Here, the norm on the left-hand side denotes the maximum value of ''f'' in the closed disc:

:<math> \|f\|_r = \max_{|z| \le r} |f(z)| =  \max_{|z| = r} |f(z)|</math>

(where the last equality is due to the maximum modulus principle).

== Proof ==

Define ''A'' by

: <math> A = \sup_{|z| \le R} \operatorname{Re} f(z). </math>

If ''f'' is constant ''c'', the inequality follows from <math>(R+r)|c|+2r\operatorname{Re}c\ge(R-r)|c|</math>, so we may assume ''f'' is nonconstant. First let ''f''(0) = 0. Since Re ''f'' is harmonic, Re ''f''(0) is equal to the average of its values around any circle centered at 0. That is,

: <math> \operatorname{Re} f(0) = \int_0^1 \operatorname{Re} f(R{\rm e}^{2\pi{\rm i} s}){\,\rm d}s. </math>

Since ''f'' is regular and nonconstant, we have that Re ''f'' is also nonconstant. Since Re ''f''(0) = 0, we must have Re <math> f(z) > 0 </math> for some ''z'' on the circle <math>|z|=R</math>, so we may take <math>A>0</math>. Now ''f'' maps into the half-plane ''P'' to the left of the ''x''=''A'' line. Roughly, our goal is to map this half-plane to a disk, apply [[Schwarz's lemma]] there, and make out the stated inequality.

<math>w \mapsto w/A - 1</math> sends ''P'' to the standard left half-plane. <math>w \mapsto R(w+1)/(w-1)</math> sends the left half-plane to the circle of radius ''R'' centered at the origin. The composite, which maps 0 to 0, is the desired map:

:<math>w \mapsto \frac{Rw}{w-2A}.</math>

From Schwarz's lemma applied to the composite of this map and ''f'', we have

:<math>\frac{|Rf(z)|}{|f(z)-2A|} \leq |z|.</math>

Take |''z''| &le; ''r''. The above becomes

:<math>R|f(z)| \leq r|f(z) - 2A| \leq r|f(z)| + 2Ar</math>

so

:<math>|f(z)| \leq \frac{2Ar}{R-r}</math>,

as claimed. In the general case, we may apply the above to ''f''(''z'')-''f''(0):

:<math>
\begin{align}
  |f(z)|-|f(0)|
    &\leq |f(z)-f(0)|
     \leq \frac{2r}{R-r} \sup_{|w| \leq R} \operatorname{Re}(f(w) - f(0)) \\
    &\leq \frac{2r}{R-r} \left(\sup_{|w| \leq R} \operatorname{Re} f(w) + |f(0)|\right),
\end{align}</math>

which, when rearranged, gives the claim.

== Alternative result and proof ==
We start with the following result:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ishita Goluguri, Toyesh Jayaswal, Andrew Lee |title=The Prime Number Theorem: A PRIMES Exposition |url=https://math.mit.edu/research/highschool/primes/materials/2020/December/6-Goluguri-Jayaswal-Lee.pdf }}</ref>

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem
| note = 
| math_statement = If <math>f = u + iv</math> is analytic on <math>B(0, R+\epsilon)</math> for some <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, and <math>u \leq M</math> on <math>\partial B(0, R)</math>, then <math>\forall n\geq 1</math>,

<math display="block">|f^{(n)}(0) | \leq \frac{2n!}{R^n} (M -u(0))</math>

and similarly if <math>v \leq M</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof<ref>{{Cite web |last=Liu |first=Travor |title=Borel-Caratheodory Lemma and Its Application |date=16 February 2021 |url=https://travorlzh.github.io/2021/02/16/borel-caratheodory-lemma.html}}</ref>|proof= 

It suffices to prove the <math>u</math> case, since the <math>v</math> case is found by <math>-if = v - iu</math>.

WLOG, subtract a constant away, to get <math>f(0) = 0</math>.

Do three contour integrals around <math>\partial B(0, R)</math> using Cauchy integral formula:

<math display="block">f^{(n)}(0)/n! =\frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint \frac{f(z)}{z^{n+1}}dz =  \int_0^1 \frac{f(Re^{2\pi i t})}{R^ne^{2\pi in t} }dt</math>

<math display="block">\int_0^1 f(Re^{2\pi i t}) e^{2\pi int}dt = \frac{1}{2\pi i R^n}\oint f(z) z^{n-1}dz = 0</math>

<math display="block">\int_0^1 f(Re^{2\pi i t})dt = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint f(z) z^{-1}dz = f(0) = 0</math>

Pick angle <math>\theta</math>, so that <math>e^{-i\theta} f^{(n)}(0) = | f^{(n)}(0)|</math>. Then by linearly combining the three integrals, we get

<math display="block">\int_0^1 f(Re^{2\pi i t})dt (1 +  \cos(2\pi nt + \theta)) = \frac 12 R^n |f^{(n)} (0)|/n!</math>

The imaginary part vanishes, and the real part gives

<math display="block">\int_0^1 u(Re^{2\pi i t})dt (1 +  \cos(2\pi nt + \theta)) = \frac 12 R^n |f^{(n)} (0)|/n!</math>

The integral is bounded above by <math>M\int_0^1 dt (1 +  \cos(2\pi nt + \theta))  = M</math>, so we have the result.
}}

{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary 1
| note = 
| math_statement = With the same assumptions, for all <math>r\in (0, R)</math>,

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \partial B(0, r)}| f(z)| \leq \frac{2r}{R-r} M + \frac{R+r}{R-r}|f(0)|</math>
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=  

It suffices to prove the case of <math>f(0) = 0</math>.

By previous result, using the Taylor expansion,

<math display="block">|f(z)| \leq \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!}|f^{(n)}(0)|\cdot |z|^n \leq |f(0)| + \sum_{n=1}^\infty2M (r/R)^n  = \frac{2r}{R-r} M </math>
}}
{{Math theorem|name = Corollary 2
| note = Titchmarsh, 5.51, improved|math_statement=  
With the same assumptions, for all <math>r\in (0, R)</math>, and all integer <math>n\geq 1</math>

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \partial B(0, r)}| f^{(n)}(z)| \leq \frac{2n!}{(R-r)^{n+1}} R(M- u(0))</math>
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=  

It suffices to prove the case of <math>f(0) = 0</math> as well. And similarly to above,
<math display="block">	  \begin{align}
	  |f^{(n)}(z)| &\leq \sum_{k=n}^\infty \frac{k\cdots (k-n+1)}{k!}|f^{(k)}(0)|\cdot |z|^{k-n}  \\
	  &\leq \frac{2(M - u(0))}{R^n}\sum_{k=n}^\infty k\cdots (k-n+1) \left(\frac rR\right)^{k-n} \\
	  &= \frac{2n!}{(R-r)^{n+1}} R(M- u(0))
	  \end{align}
</math>
}}

<!--
{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary 2
| note = Titchmarsh, 5.51
| math_statement = With the same assumptions, for all <math>r\in (0, R)</math>,

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \partial B(0, r)}| f^{(n)}(z)| \leq \frac{2^n n!}{(R-r)^{n+1}}((2R + 2r) M + (3R + r)|f(0)| )</math>
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=  

For any <math>z\in \partial B(0, r)</math>, we use Cauchy integral formula around a circle of radius <math>\frac{R-r}{2}</math>, centered on <math>z</math>, to obtain:

<math display="block">|f^{(n)}(z)| \leq \frac{n!}{2\pi} \oint \frac{|f(w)|}{|w-z|^{n+1}}dw \leq \frac{2^nn!}{(R-r)^n}\max_{z\in \bar B(0, (r+R)/2)}| f(z)|</math>

To bound <math>\max_{z\in \bar B(0, (r+R)/2)}| f(z)|</math>, we notice that the upper bound in the previous result monotonically increases as the radius goes up from <math>0</math> to <math>R</math>, so we have

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \bar B(0, (r+R)/2)}| f(z)| \leq  \frac{2(r+R)/2}{R-(r+R)/2} M + \frac{R+(r+R)/2}{R-(r+R)/2}|f(0)|</math>

}}
-->


== Applications ==
Borel–Carathéodory is often used to bound the logarithm of derivatives, such as in the proof of [[Hadamard factorization theorem]].

The following example is a strengthening of [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem]].

{{Math theorem
| name = Liouville's theorem, improved
| note = 
| math_statement = If <math>f</math> is an entire function, such that there exists a sequence <math>r_k \nearrow \infty</math> with <math>\max_{z \in \partial B(0, r_k)} \Re(f(z)) = o(r_k^{n+1})</math>, then <math>f</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>n</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
By Borel-Caratheodory lemma, for any <math>0 < r< r_k</math>,

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \partial B(0, r)}| f^{(n+1)}(z)| \leq \frac{4n!}{(r_k-r)^{n+2}} r_k M</math>
	  where <math>M = \max_{z\in \partial B(0, r_k)} \Re(f(z)) = o(r_k^{n+1})</math>.  

Letting <math>r \leq \frac{r_k}{2}</math>, and taking the <math>k \nearrow \infty</math> limit:

<math display="block">\max_{z\in \partial B(0, r)}| f^{(n+1)}(z)| = o(1) \to 0</math>

Thus by Liouville's theorem, <math>f^{(n+1)}</math> is a constant function, and it converges to zero, so it is zero. So <math>f</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>n</math>.
}}

{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary
| note
| math_statement = If an entire function <math>f</math> has no roots and is of finite [[Entire function#Order and type|order]] <math>\rho</math>, then <math>f(z) = e^{p(z)}</math> for some polynomial <math>p</math> of degree <math>\deg(p) \leq \rho</math>.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
Apply the improved Liouville theorem to <math>g = \log(f)</math>.
}}
